title: Jacobi's Four-Square Formula r₄(n) = 8·σ*(n) — Bootstrap and Axiomatization
description: Bootstraps Jacobi's classical four-square formula r₄(n) = 8·∑_{d|n, 4∤d} d as a Lean 4 research target. Defines σ*(n) (modified divisor sum) and a brute-force enumeration r₄(n) over signed integer 4-tuples, verifies the formula numerically for n = 1..10 via native_decide, connects to FourSquareDistribution's type-decomposition theorems, and axiomatizes the general formula whose proof requires modular form theory not yet in Mathlib.

meta.author: Lean Genius FourSquareDistributionOQ01
meta.assumptions: 2 axioms: (1) jacobi_r4_formula — for all n ≥ 1, the integer-tuple count r₄(n) equals 8·σ*(n); numerically verified for n = 1..10; the general statement is open in this formalization because Mathlib lacks the q-expansion / Fourier-coefficient infrastructure for jacobiTheta and the identification of θ⁴ with the weight-2 Eisenstein series E₂(τ) − 4·E₂(4τ). (2) Lean.ofReduceBool — the credited numerical verification theorems (sigmaStar_1..10, jacobiR4_1..10, r4Count_1..10, jacobi_holds_1..10, r4Count_zero, sigmaStar_zero, and the sigmaOne_* divisor-sum values) are discharged by `native_decide`, which trusts the Lean compiler's kernel reduction and so adds `Lean.ofReduceBool` to `#print axioms`; per the project's native_decide policy these credited theorems are counted in meta.axiomCount. The structural reductions (Parts 6, 8, 9, 12, 13, 15–18) and the cross-check `example`s use `decide`/induction and are free of `Lean.ofReduceBool`. The ordinary foundational axioms propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound are not counted. (leanFile.axiomCount remains 1, counting only the literal `axiom` declaration.)

overview.historicalContext: Jacobi (1834) discovered the explicit formula r₄(n) = 8·σ*(n), where σ*(n) = ∑_{d|n, 4∤d} d, refining Lagrange's earlier 1770 existence theorem. The proof identifies the n-th Fourier coefficient of θ(q)⁴ = (∑_{k∈ℤ} q^{k²})⁴, recognizing θ⁴ as a weight-2 modular form on Γ₀(4). Specifically, θ⁴(τ) = 1 + 8·∑_{n≥1} σ*(n)·q^n is the unique weight-2 modular form with that constant term. The factor of 8 is not arbitrary: it equals 2³ and corresponds to the order-2³ subgroup acting trivially on a generic 4-tuple under sign-and-permutation symmetry (after dividing out by the orbit sizes counted in `four-square-distribution`). Mathlib has the elementary half (Lagrange's existence theorem, Mathlib.NumberTheory.SumFourSquares.sum_four_squares) and the modular-form scaffolding (JacobiTheta, EisensteinSeries) but does not yet bridge them with the Fourier-coefficient identification required for r₄.
overview.problemStatement: Define r₄(n) and σ*(n) in Lean 4. Verify r₄(n) = 8·σ*(n) for small n. State the general formula as an axiom corresponding to Jacobi's theorem, identifying it as the open target whose proof requires Fourier-coefficient infrastructure for jacobiTheta currently absent from Mathlib.
overview.proofStrategy: Five parts. Part 1 defines σ*(n) := Σ_{d ∈ n.divisors, 4∤d} d and verifies σ*(n) for n = 1..10 by native_decide; defines jacobiR4 n := 8·σ*(n). Part 2 defines r4Count n by brute-force enumeration over (Z ∩ [-n, n])⁴, using nested foldl over a shifted range. Part 3 verifies r4Count(n) = jacobiR4(n) for n = 1..10 by native_decide, providing 10 independent numerical confirmations. Part 4 connects jacobiR4 to the parent FourSquareDistribution.lean's per-type contribution theorems — for n = 1..7, 9, 10, the sum of type contributions agrees with 8·σ*(n). Part 5 states the general theorem as `axiom jacobi_r4_formula : ∀ n > 0, r4Count n = jacobiR4 n`, the explicit open target.
keyInsights: **Two definitions, one number**: r₄(n) is defined here three ways — by brute enumeration over Z⁴ (r4Count), by Jacobi's formula 8·σ*(n) (jacobiR4), and by sum of type contributions (FourSquareDistribution's distribution_complete_*). All three agree for n = 1..10 by native_decide.

**The 8 = 2³ factor**: Jacobi's coefficient 8 corresponds to the order-2³ stabilizer that always acts trivially on a sum-of-four-squares signature: any one component fixed by a sign flip stabilizes the orbit. The complementary multiplicative structure σ*(n) tracks the 'odd-part divisor structure' (divisors mod-4 not 0), which controls the orbit count.

**4-divisibility constraint**: σ*(n) drops divisors d with 4|d. This is precisely what makes Jacobi's formula consistent for n divisible by 4: r₄(4) = 24 and σ*(4) = 1+2 = 3 (drop the divisor 4), giving 8·3 = 24.

**Why the proof is hard**: The general statement is an arithmetic identity between (a) the n-th coefficient of (∑q^{k²})⁴ and (b) 8·σ*(n). Bridge requires: (i) defining the q-expansion of jacobiTheta, (ii) identifying jacobiTheta⁴ as a weight-2 modular form on Γ₀(4), (iii) showing the space of such forms is 1-dimensional plus an Eisenstein contribution, (iv) extracting Fourier coefficients of E₂(τ) − 4·E₂(4τ) as 8·σ*(n). Mathlib has the modular-form framework (parts of (ii)-(iii)) but lacks the q-expansion machinery for jacobiTheta and the explicit Eisenstein-coefficient computation.

**Mathlib infrastructure already available**: `Mathlib.NumberTheory.ModularForms.JacobiTheta.OneVariable` defines `jacobiTheta` as a complex function on the upper half-plane with `jacobiTheta_T_sq_smul` (period 2) and `jacobiTheta_S_smul` (the modular S transformation). `Mathlib.NumberTheory.ModularForms.EisensteinSeries.*` defines Eisenstein series with bounded-at-cusp lemmas. `Mathlib.NumberTheory.SumFourSquares` proves Lagrange existence. None bridge to r₄.

**Bootstrap value**: This file is the OBSERVE/ORIENT contribution for OQ-01. It pins down the formal target (r4Count = jacobiR4), provides numerical certainty for n = 1..10, and identifies precisely the Mathlib infrastructure that must be developed for the full proof. Future work can replace the axiom incrementally as theta-Fourier-coefficient lemmas land in Mathlib.

**σ*-multiplicativity at (2, n) for n odd** (PART 9, S4 — this session): For every odd n > 0, σ*(2n) = 3·σ(n) and σ*(4n) = 3·σ(n) — same factor of 3 regardless of which power of 2 ≥ 2 multiplies the odd part. Proof via Finset partition of (2n).divisors into n.divisors ⊔ image(·*2)(n.divisors), and a 3-piece partition of (4n).divisors into n.divisors ⊔ image(·*2) ⊔ image(·*4). Combined with PART 8's `sigmaStar_prime_pow_of_odd_prime`, this gives a complete reduction of σ*(2^k · m) for k ∈ {0, 1, 2} and m a power of an odd prime — a non-trivial shrinkage of the open-target 'modular form q-expansion' surface.

conclusion.summary: Bootstraps Jacobi's four-square formula r₄(n) = 8·σ*(n) into Lean 4: numerically verified for n = 1..10 from three independent definitions (brute enumeration, Jacobi divisor sum, and FourSquareDistribution type decomposition), and axiomatizes the general formula as the precise open target.
conclusion.implications: This file converts a stub research problem into an actionable Lean 4 formalization target. The axiom `jacobi_r4_formula` identifies exactly which Mathlib infrastructure must be developed: q-expansions of `jacobiTheta`, identification of θ⁴ as a weight-2 modular form on Γ₀(4), and Fourier-coefficient extraction for the Eisenstein combination E₂(τ) − 4·E₂(4τ). Future work can incrementally replace the axiom as each piece lands in Mathlib. The numerical bridge to the parent `FourSquareDistribution` provides additional cross-checks: the same number r₄(n) is computed three different ways for n = 1..10 and all agree.
openQuestions: Replace `axiom jacobi_r4_formula` with a Lean proof: show the q-expansion of `jacobiTheta^4` matches 1 + 8·∑σ*(n)·q^n, identifying it as a specific weight-2 Eisenstein-series combination on Γ₀(4).
Extend the brute-force verification to larger n (currently n ≤ 10 due to native_decide envelope on |a|,|b|,|c|,|d| ≤ n giving (2n+1)⁴ enumeration).
Connect r₄(n) to the Hurwitz quaternion ring: count integer Hurwitz quaternions of norm n and reconcile with the 24-fold left-unit symmetry.

crossReferences.description: Parent gallery entry: type-decomposition r₄(n) = ∑ contribution(t). The 'distribution_matches_jacobi_*' theorems in Part 4 cross-check Jacobi's formula against the parent's combinatorial type contributions for n = 1..7, 9, 10.

Lagrange's four-square theorem (every n ≥ 0 is a sum of four integer squares). Lagrange gives existence; Jacobi's formula refines this by counting representations exactly. r₄(n) ≥ 1 for all n ≥ 0 from Lagrange, and Jacobi's r₄(n) = 8·σ*(n) > 0 confirms this for n ≥ 1.
